name: Amira Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary site day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crew that cranes factory-built house modules onto foundations and finishes the joins. My trade certificate taught me the timber work, and years on muddy sites taught me to watch the crane, lorry and ground together. I like the moment two halves finally become one house.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is happening at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Gabor runs a small electrical business, and we have two children in school, a mortgage and about three months saved. I use AI every day to check weather, lorry times and crane bookings. The first wrong delivery can lose us a whole paid morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the modular crew my daily AI schedule is still useful, even if the wider claims are noise. It catches a lorry arriving before the crane is ready, which saves us a lot of standing around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gabor’s electrical business brings in money and we have a few months saved. My site lead pay is ordinary, the mortgage and two children’s school costs are real, and a plateau leaves the household broadly steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting modular units onto foundations and checking the lifting points against the delivery sheet. I would use the same AI clash list each morning and leave our present savings transfer at its current rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A good building day has enough surprises without asking a computer to invent more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first check on a unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lifting eyes and the number painted on the side. A wrong module on the hook can waste the crane slot before anyone fixes a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start the business you have mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Gabor and I have talked about our own modular firm, but we have not priced a shed or a crew. A plateau alone does not fund it.

say: I would keep using the existing **AI clash list** for lorries and crane time.
I would remind the crew that **lifting checks** still happen beside the module.
think: Gabor’s business and our **few months saved** make the current household secure.
An independent **modular firm** is only an idea, without priced space or workers.
do: Keep setting **modular units** and checking lifting points against delivery sheets.
Continue the existing **daily AI schedule** and current savings amount.
feel: **Calm** about income, with normal building-site surprises.
S0.quote: A wrong module on the hook can waste the crane slot before anyone fixes a wall.
fieldNote: Her daily AI use is **already normal work**, not a newly learned skill.
The business idea remains unpriced, and her **moderate cushion** supports a calm baseline.

steps.text: Keep modular lifts and verify units against delivery sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster buying and booking might help, but the crane crew needs a human stop call when the road is blocked. I would ask the company to test the new AI delivery screen on one real site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office planners may lose work while my on-site lifting continues. The contractor might also shorten the paid waiting time between modules, which would trim my wage; Gabor’s electrical bookings could fluctuate if his customers cut building work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI delivery controls with the dispatcher once the company gives me access. I would log two blocked-road mistakes, and if paid waiting hours fall for three rosters, Gabor and I would postpone the kitchen refit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both wages possibly thinning, even with a few months put aside. I would rather measure the hours before spending on a new kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you log about a blocked road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time, module number and which driver had to turn around. I want a repairable error, not a complaint that disappears at the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the kitchen first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old cupboards still work while the mortgage cannot wait. If either of us loses paid hours, a new kitchen can wait.

say: I would ask for a **real-site trial** before AI delivery screens control module lifts.
I would keep a **human stop call** when a road or crane slot changes.
think: My **waiting pay** could shrink under tighter schedules.
Gabor’s **electrical bookings** might also weaken if building customers pull back.
do: Learn new **AI delivery controls** with company access and record blocked-road errors.
Postpone the **kitchen refit** if three rosters show lower paid waiting hours.
feel: **Anxious** about possible loss in either household wage.
S1.quote: The old cupboards still work while the mortgage cannot wait.
fieldNote: She accepts a new tool but tests it against **real access failures**.
The kitchen delay is conditional on **three weaker rosters**, and household income includes Gabor’s business.

steps.text: Learn new AI delivery controls with company access and log blocked-road errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site that thinking AI in 2028 can arrange the lorries, but it cannot guide a house module onto its base. Around 2031 capable robots may do that, and I want trials with power off before a live lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some site positions to go once robots handle the final alignment. My own lead hours could shrink, while Gabor’s business may face cheaper automated quotes; our few months saved cannot carry both incomes for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay with paid modular shifts and ask for a posted robot-lift supervisor role with funded training on paid time. If that posted role pays enough for our mortgage, I would complete the course and apply; if not, I would search posted nearby building roles only after the first real cut to my paid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed about two possible income cuts. I have a route to try, but both jobs matter at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test with power off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would isolate the robot and crane controls before marking the exclusion zone and rehearsing a stop call. Only a qualified operator would power them for a supervised trial with no one under the module.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for any supervisor title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A supervisor title with fewer paid hours would not cover the mortgage. I need a posted role, a firm wage and a safe training schedule.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** schedules modules before 2031 robots can align them on site.
I would start with **isolated controls** and a rehearsed stop before supervised lift trials.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink once capable robots handle alignment.
Gabor’s **business revenue** may also fall if automated quotes reshape building work.
do: Complete **funded robot-lift training** only for a posted mortgage-covering supervisor role with paid time.
Search **posted nearby building jobs** after a real cut to paid days if no suitable role appears.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts to both household incomes, while retaining several options.
S2.quote: A supervisor title with fewer paid hours would not cover the mortgage.
fieldNote: Her training depends on **posted work** with firm pay and paid time.
The safe trial starts with **dead equipment**, then supervised operation away from workers under modules.

steps.text: Keep paid modular installation shifts while available
Complete funded robot-lift course only for posted mortgage-covering role with paid time
Search posted nearby building jobs after paid days fall if no suitable supervisor role appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the crew time to test alignment robots on uneven bases and in wind. A showroom fit is not a house in rain with a lorry waiting at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may handle plans first, while robots reach the hands-on lift around 2034. I will be fifty one with children still growing and a mortgage; a funded controls skill could protect my job if the company creates a paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running module lifts this year and offer to join a paid two-week alignment trial if the contractor schedules one. I would learn the new controls, record each failed stop and apply for a posted operator vacancy only if its wage and hours cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy in a useful way. More time lets me learn with the machine instead of meeting it after the crew has been cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you halt a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A module shifting after the stop call or a worker entering the marked swing area. I would stop, isolate the equipment and record the exact motion before anyone powers it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the trial yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The company owns the crane and the robot; the two-week test and control training should be paid work, not a hobby charged to our savings.

say: I would demand **uneven-base trials** before 2034 alignment robots reach live sites.
I would record **failed stops** and stop work before anyone restarts unsafe equipment.
think: I will need **paid site work** at fifty one when robots arrive.
A funded **controls role** could help if the company actually posts it.
do: Join a **paid two-week robot trial** if scheduled and learn the new alignment controls.
Apply for a **posted operator vacancy** only if firm hours and wage cover the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about future job shape, with paid time to learn if offered.
S3.quote: A showroom fit is not a house in rain with a lorry waiting at the gate.
fieldNote: She treats the trial as **paid company work** and records failed stops before restarting.
The operator application remains conditional on **posted hours** and mortgage-covering pay.

steps.text: Join paid two-week robot trial if scheduled and learn alignment controls
Apply for posted operator job only if firm hours and pay cover mortgage
Stop and isolate equipment after unsafe motion; record fault before restarting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices they can learn to finish a module by hand before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. Ten years is long enough to build a real trade, not just tap a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty six when robots do the hands-on alignment, and I may still need my site wage. Gabor’s business and our savings give some room, but I will not count a future modular company of our own until it has paying customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the modular crew working during 2026 and move an extra amount from each paid month into savings if our mortgage and school costs are covered. In the first year after 2036 I would review actual site hours and any posted operator vacancies before changing jobs; by 2039 I would take only a paid role that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant work change, calm enough to plan from today’s wages. I want the children to see us build something that stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra could you put away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty from a paid month if Gabor’s bookings and our core bills allow it. I would not shift existing savings between accounts and call that preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start your own firm now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have not priced a workshop or a crew, and there is no customer list. I would keep my wage until our modular business is more than a sketch.

say: I would protect **hands-on modular training** before 2036 plans and 2039 robots change sites.
I would teach apprentices that **trade judgement** is more than an app screen.
think: I may still need **site wages** when robots reach alignment work around 2039.
An independent **modular firm** is an idea, not income without paying customers.
do: Keep **2026 modular crew** shifts while paid work remains.
Save an extra **thirty monthly** only if Gabor’s bookings and core bills allow.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant job change, with present household income steady.
S4.quote: I would keep my wage until our modular business is more than a sketch.
fieldNote: She names actual **new saving from wages**, conditional on the second income and core bills.
The business dream is deliberately excluded from action tags because it has **no priced plan** or customers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because alignment robots could cut my site hours by 2031 while Gabor’s customer work might also change. Posted paid supervisor work, funded training on paid time and safe power-off trials would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who has the authority to stop a robot lift. A house can be rebuilt; a worker under the module cannot.

headlineQuote: A house can be rebuilt; a worker under the module cannot.
portrait: **Amira**, 43, leads modular house installation with a trade certificate, typical pay, three months saved and some nearby site jobs.
She and Gabor support **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with his electrical business providing a second income.
She uses **AI daily** and would learn robot controls through paid trials with isolated equipment and clear stop authority.
The **2028 case** worries her because her site hours and Gabor’s bookings could both weaken.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink modular site hours around 2031 alongside Gabor’s customer work.
whatWouldHelp: **Posted paid roles**, funded training and isolated-equipment trials would help her respond.
